build_mogen(): choosing an order instead of assuming one

honets

2026-08-26

The analytic question

build_hon() decides per context whether memory is warranted. build_mogen() asks the question at the level of the whole model: fit Markov chains of every order from 0 up to max_order, score each one, and report which order the data actually support.

The multi-order model of Scholtes (2017) treats the layers as a nested family — each order’s likelihood is computed on the paths it can explain, with the degrees of freedom that order costs — so the comparison is a like-for-like model selection rather than a race between separately-fitted models.

library(honets)
seqs <- split(human_long$code, human_long$session_id)
library(cograph)

Fitting

mo <- build_mogen(seqs, max_order = 4)
mo
Multi-Order Generative Model (MOGen)
  Optimal order:  4 (by aic)
  Orders tested:  0 to 4
  States:         9
  Paths:          425 (10792 observations)
  AIC:            44078.7 | 41818.8 | 41084.3 | 40684.5 | 35293.7*
  BIC:            44137.0 | 42401.7* | 46192.1 | 63848.5 | 81060.6
  (* = minimum;  AIC favors order 4, BIC favors order 1)

The print method flags the minimum of each criterion, and here they disagree: AIC selects order 4, BIC selects order 1. The asterisks make the disagreement visible rather than hiding it behind a single “optimal order”.

The selection table

as.data.frame(mo)
  order log_likelihood      aic      bic  dof layer_dof optimal
1     0      -22031.34 44078.69 44136.98    8         8   FALSE
2     1      -20829.39 41818.79 42401.71   80        72   FALSE
3     2      -19841.13 41084.25 46192.13  701       621   FALSE
4     3      -17163.27 40684.54 63848.51 3179      2478   FALSE
5     4      -11365.83 35293.66 81060.55 6281      3102    TRUE

The dof column explains everything. Going from order 3 to order 4 adds 3,102 parameters (layer_dof) on 10,792 observations. The log-likelihood improves substantially — from −17,163 to −11,366 — so AIC, which charges 2 per parameter, is delighted. BIC charges log(10792) ≈ 9.3 per parameter and is appalled: its score rises from 42,402 at order 1 to 81,061 at order 4.

optimal marks the order selected under the criterion you asked for (criterion = "aic" by default).

Seeing the selection

plot() draws both information criteria against order, marking the selected one. The AIC and BIC curves crossing in different places is the disagreement the next section discusses.

plot(mo)

Which criterion should you use?

It depends on what the model is for.

  • Describing the corpus — AIC. You want the order that best captures the structure actually present, and over-parameterisation is a cost you are willing to pay for fidelity.
  • Claiming the process is order-k — BIC. It is consistent for model identification, and its verdict of order 1 is a real warning that a fourth-order chain is not identifiable from 425 sessions.
  • Testing whether order k improves on k−1 — neither; use markov_order_test(), which calibrates the likelihood-ratio statistic against a permutation null rather than an information criterion.
mo_bic <- build_mogen(seqs, max_order = 4, criterion = "bic")
mo_bic$optimal_order
[1] 1

Switching the criterion changes the selected order, and it should be reported alongside the result.

The fitted transitions

mogen_transitions() is the tidy accessor for the fitted layer.

mogen_transitions(mo, top = 5)
                                                   path count probability
1 Specify -> Command -> Request -> Specify -> Interrupt   127      0.7175
2 Specify -> Command -> Specify -> Interrupt -> Command    48      0.3902
3 Command -> Request -> Specify -> Interrupt -> Command    37      0.2721
4   Command -> Command -> Command -> Command -> Command    27      0.3803
5  Command -> Request -> Specify -> Interrupt -> Verify    27      0.1985
                                        from        to
1   Specify -> Command -> Request -> Specify Interrupt
2 Specify -> Command -> Specify -> Interrupt   Command
3 Command -> Request -> Specify -> Interrupt   Command
4   Command -> Command -> Command -> Command   Command
5 Command -> Request -> Specify -> Interrupt    Verify

At order 4, a “state” is a four-step history. The heaviest is Specify -> Command -> Request -> Specify continuing to Interrupt, 127 times at probability 0.72 — a highly deterministic recurring routine, and the kind of structure that only a high-order layer can express.

The same table is reachable through the standard accessor, and order = selects a different layer:

as.data.frame(mo, what = "transitions", order = 2, top = 4)
                             path count probability               from
1   Specify -> Command -> Specify   284      0.3901 Specify -> Command
2   Command -> Request -> Specify   231      0.7649 Command -> Request
3   Specify -> Command -> Request   199      0.2734 Specify -> Command
4 Request -> Specify -> Interrupt   189      0.3259 Request -> Specify
         to
1   Specify
2   Specify
3   Request
4 Interrupt

The fitted layer as shape

plot_simplicial() takes a mogen_transitions() table directly through pathways =, so the fitted second-order layer can be read as shape over the network rather than as 702 rows. The network it draws on is the first-order one — nine states. Because mogen_transitions() returns rows already sorted by count, top = N picks the N heaviest.

net1 <- build_hon(seqs, max_order = 1)
plot_simplicial(net1, pathways = mogen_transitions(mo, order = 2, top = 6),
                max_pathways = 6,
                title = "Six heaviest second-order pathways")

A single pathway, isolated:

plot_simplicial(net1, pathways = mogen_transitions(mo, order = 2, top = 1),
                max_pathways = 1)

Path counts without fitting a model

path_counts() is the descriptive counterpart: how often does each k-step path occur, with no model behind it.

path_counts(seqs, k = 3, top = 6)
                             path count proportion
1   Specify -> Command -> Specify   284     0.0286
2   Command -> Request -> Specify   231     0.0232
3   Specify -> Command -> Request   199     0.0200
4 Request -> Specify -> Interrupt   189     0.0190
5   Command -> Command -> Command   177     0.0178
6 Command -> Specify -> Interrupt   149     0.0150

Useful as a sanity check before fitting, and for reporting the raw evidence under a modelled claim.

A caution on max_order

Raising max_order is not free. The parameter count grows roughly as |S|^(k+1), and past a certain point the higher layers are fitting individual sequences.

do.call(rbind, lapply(2:4, function(k) {
  m <- build_mogen(seqs, max_order = k)
  d <- as.data.frame(m)
  data.frame(max_order = k, selected_aic = m$optimal_order,
             top_layer_dof = max(d$layer_dof))
}))
  max_order selected_aic top_layer_dof
1         2            2           621
2         3            3          2478
3         4            4          3102

If AIC keeps selecting whatever ceiling you set, that is a sign the ceiling is doing the choosing, not the data. Check BIC and the permutation test before believing it.

What to do next

  • markov_order_test() — the permutation-based version of this question, which does not rely on an information criterion.
  • build_hon() — per-context order selection instead of one order for the whole model.
  • build_hypa() — which specific paths occur more or less often than a null model expects.
  • pathways() — hand the fitted model’s paths to the simplicial and hypergraph families.

References

  • Scholtes, I. (2017). When is a network a network? Multi-order graphical model selection in pathways and temporal networks. KDD 2017, 1037-1046.
  • Gote, C., & Scholtes, I. (2023). Predicting sequences of traversed nodes in graphs using network models with multiple higher orders. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery.
